Instead of generating text one token at a time, which is slow because each step requires a full forward pass through the model, speculative decoding uses a smaller, faster "draft" model to predict a sequence of tokens. The main, larger model then evaluates this entire sequence in a single pass.

If the main model agrees with the draft model’s predictions, the entire sequence is accepted, and the process moves to the next chunk. If the main model disagrees at any point, it rejects the draft from that point onward and generates the correct token itself, after which the process restarts.

The key to your question is why this doesn’t change the output. The main model is the source of truth. It is never asked to "guess" or "hallucinate" new content; it is only asked to verify or correct the draft. Because the main model’s output is deterministic (or sampled from its own probability distribution) based on the context, and it is the final arbiter of every token, the final text is identical to what the main model would have produced if it had generated every token sequentially. The draft model is merely a proposal engine; it has no authority over the final text.

If the draft is right, the main model accepts it. There is no approximation or lossy compression involved in the final output. The speedup comes from parallelizing the verification of multiple tokens, not from changing the model’s logic.

When a hash map is asked to store a key, it first runs that key through a hash function, which produces a number. That number gets reduced to an index into an internal array by taking a modulus with the array's size, so even if the hash function spits out a huge integer, you always land somewhere in the array. The problem is that different keys can produce the same index — this is a collision, and it's not some rare edge case; by the pigeonhole principle, it's mathematically guaranteed once the number of stored keys exceeds the number of slots.

There are two broad strategies for dealing with it. The most common, used in languages like Java's HashMap and Python's dict, is chaining: each slot in the array holds not a single entry but a small linked list (or, in some implementations, a tiny array) of all entries that hashed to that slot. To look up a key, you go to the computed slot and walk through the short list until you find a matching key. This keeps insertion and deletion straightforward, because you're just adding or removing a node from a list. The other broad strategy is open addressing: instead of keeping a separate list, you leave the slot empty if it's occupied and probe for the next empty one according to some rule — the next slot over (linear probing), then two slots over, then four (quadratic), or a secondary hash function to jump around (double hashing). Open addressing keeps everything in one contiguous array, which can be cache-friendly, but it tends to degrade performance quickly as the table fills up because probing chains get long and the array can never be more than about half full.

The map only resizes when it gets too full. The rule is expressed in terms of a load factor, which is simply the number of stored entries divided by the number of slots. When the load factor crosses a threshold — commonly 0.7 in mainstream implementations — the map concludes that collisions are now happening too often and lookups will start taking longer than they should. It allocates a new array, typically twice the old size (or the next prime number that's larger, depending on the implementation), and then takes every single existing entry, recomputes its index in the new, larger array, and reinserts it. This reinsertion can even resolve some collisions that existed before, because the keys are now spread across more slots. The whole operation costs proportional to the number of entries in play, so it's an expensive O(n) step. However, because resizes are relatively rare relative to the sheer number of ordinary put and get operations that happen between them, the cost averages out to a constant over time, which is what people mean when they say hash-map operations are "amortized O(1)."

A hash map stores key-value pairs by first running the key through a hash function, which produces an integer that serves as an index into an array of slots called a table or buckets.
